content: Before initiating therapy with cefprozil, it is essential to thoroughly assess the patient’s history of hypersensitivity reactions to cefprozil, cephalosporins, penicillins, or other drugs. If cefprozil is prescribed to patients with a known penicillin allergy, caution is advised due to the documented cross-sensitivity among β-lactam antibiotics, which can occur in up to 10% of such patients. If an allergic reaction to cefprozil occurs, the drug should be discontinued immediately. Severe acute hypersensitivity reactions may necessitate emergency interventions, including administration of epinephrine, oxygen, intravenous fluids, antihistamines, corticosteroids, vasopressors, and airway management, as clinically indicated. Clostridium difficile-associated diarrhea (CDAD) has been reported with nearly all antibacterial agents, including cefprozil, and can range from mild diarrhea to fatal colitis. Antibacterial therapy disrupts the normal flora of the colon, leading to overgrowth of C. difficile, which produces toxins A and B that contribute to CDAD. Hypertoxin-producing strains of C. difficile are associated with increased morbidity and mortality, as these infections may be resistant to antimicrobial therapy and could require colectomy. CDAD should be considered in all patients presenting with diarrhea following antibiotic use, and a detailed medical history is necessary since CDAD can occur up to two months after antibiotic administration. If CDAD is suspected or confirmed, discontinuation of ongoing antibiotic use not directed against C. difficile may be necessary. Appropriate fluid and electrolyte management, protein supplementation, targeted antibiotic therapy for C. difficile, and surgical evaluation should be implemented as clinically indicated. Cefprozil should not be prescribed in the absence of a confirmed or strongly suspected bacterial infection or a prophylactic indication, as this increases the risk of developing drug-resistant bacteria without benefiting the patient. In patients with known or suspected renal impairment, careful clinical monitoring and appropriate laboratory studies should be conducted before and during therapy. The total daily dose of cefprozil should be reduced in such patients to avoid high or prolonged plasma antibiotic concentrations. Cephalosporins, including cefprozil, should be used cautiously in patients receiving potent diuretics, as these agents may adversely affect renal function. Prolonged use of cefprozil may lead to the overgrowth of non-susceptible organisms, necessitating close observation of the patient. If superinfection occurs, appropriate measures should be taken. Cefprozil should also be prescribed cautiously in individuals with a history of gastrointestinal disease, particularly colitis. Positive direct Coombs’ tests have been reported during treatment with cephalosporin antibiotics. Patients with phenylketonuria should be informed that cefprozil oral suspension contains phenylalanine (28 mg per 5 mL of constituted suspension for both the 125 mg/5 mL and 250 mg/5 mL dosage forms). Patients should be counseled that antibacterial drugs, including cefprozil, should only be used to treat bacterial infections and not viral infections (e.g., the common cold). When prescribed for bacterial infections, patients should be advised to complete the full course of therapy as directed, even if they feel better early in the treatment. Skipping doses or not completing the therapy may reduce the effectiveness of the treatment and increase the likelihood of bacterial resistance, making future infections harder to treat. Diarrhea is a common side effect of antibiotics and usually resolves when the antibiotic is discontinued. However, patients may develop watery and bloody stools (with or without stomach cramps and fever) even two or more months after completing the antibiotic course. If this occurs, patients should contact their physician promptly. Nephrotoxicity has been reported with the concurrent administration of aminoglycoside antibiotics and cephalosporins. Co-administration of probenecid doubles the area under the curve (AUC) for cefprozil. The bioavailability of cefprozil capsules is not affected when administered five minutes after an antacid. A false-negative reaction may occur in the ferricyanide test for blood glucose. However, the presence of cefprozil in the blood does not interfere with plasma or urine creatinine assays using the alkaline picrate method. Long-term in vivo studies to evaluate the carcinogenic potential of cefprozil have not been conducted. Cefprozil has not been found to be mutagenic in various assays, including the Ames Salmonella and E. coli WP2 uvrA reversion assays, the Chinese hamster ovary cell HGPRT forward gene mutation assay, and tests for chromosomal abnormalities or unscheduled DNA synthesis in vitro. Chromosomal aberrations were not observed in bone marrow cells from rats dosed orally with over 30 times the highest recommended human dose based on mg/m². Reproductive studies in rats and rabbits at doses up to 5 times the maximum daily human dose (1000 mg) based on mg/m² have revealed no harm to the fetus. However, there are no adequate and well-controlled studies in pregnant women, and cefprozil should only be used during pregnancy if clearly needed. Cefprozil has not been studied for use during labor and delivery, and treatment should only be given if clearly necessary. Small amounts of cefprozil (approximately 3% of the dose) have been detected in human milk following a single 1-gram dose in lactating women. Caution should be exercised when administering cefprozil to nursing women, as the effects on nursing infants are unknown. The safety and effectiveness of cefprozil in treating otitis media have been established in pediatric patients aged 6 months to 12 years. Its use for pharyngitis/tonsillitis or uncomplicated skin and skin-structure infections has been established in children aged 2 to 12 years. For acute sinusitis, safety and effectiveness have been established in children aged 6 months to 12 years. However, safety and effectiveness have not been established in pediatric patients below 6 months of age for otitis media or acute sinusitis, or below 2 years of age for pharyngitis/tonsillitis or uncomplicated skin infections. Accumulation of other cephalosporins in newborns, due to prolonged drug half-life in this age group, has been reported. In clinical studies involving over 4500 adults treated with cefprozil, 14% were aged 65 years and older, and 5% were aged 75 years and older. When elderly patients received the usual recommended adult doses, their clinical efficacy and safety were comparable to those in younger adults. However, greater sensitivity in some elderly individuals cannot be excluded. Since cefprozil is substantially excreted by the kidneys, the risk of toxic reactions may be higher in patients with impaired renal function. Elderly patients are more likely to have decreased renal function, so dose selection should be cautious, and renal function monitoring may be beneficial. Refer to dosage recommendations for patients with impaired renal function.
